problem: Standard deep RL struggles with navigation in large, visually complex multi-room environments when rewards are sparse, actions are elementary and inputs are pixels. Topological maps have growing node sets, so the state and action spaces grow dynamically, which fixed-output DQNs cannot handle.
motivation: Many practical tasks require visiting objects in a fixed sequence in large unknown environments. Humans rely on structured priors such as objects, space and maps, whereas RL agents start from scratch. Object-centric topological maps with macro actions could shrink the RL problem enough for a simple DQN to solve it.
key_idea: Build an object-centric topological map online, treat 'navigate to map node X' as a macro action, and score each node with a single-output DQN that takes the node's image patches plus a task-progress one-hot vector as input.
insight: Abstracting elementary control into object-target macro actions (A* plus a simple aiming controller) reduces the RL problem to choosing among map nodes, so a basic DQN learns within a few episodes even with terminal-only reward. The trained agent needs fewer steps per episode than a random macro-action agent, with the largest gap under terminal reward. No ablations are reported, so the individual contributions of the shared-weight multi-patch CNN, the exploration flags and the progress vector are not isolated.
method: Object-centric topological map: from RGBD and ground-truth detections, one node is created per object, storing 16x16 RGB patches, its 3D position and an explored flag. Edges come from line-of-sight or agent transitions, and waypoints are added to keep edges short.

Macro actions: an action is navigating to any node on the map, so A_t = V_t and it grows as the agent explores. A* finds the graph path and a simple controller turns toward and walks to each waypoint.
State/progress encoding: a one-hot vector x_t over the N_T targets indicates which target is currently sought, which is needed for fixed-order sequential tasks.

Variable-action DQN (DRRN-inspired): a single output neuron computes Q(f, x_t) per candidate node. N_i=10 image patches of the node go through weight-shared CNN branches, are concatenated and flattened, combined with x_t by an outer product, then passed to FC layers.
Exploration policy: with probability epsilon, a Boltzmann policy with a bonus q>0 for unexplored nodes; otherwise greedy, skipping actions already chosen (no-ops) in favour of the next-highest Q.
Multi-view training: multiple patches per object go through the same conv layers, giving more gradients per step and robustness to occlusion.

setting.backbone: Small CNN (shared weights) + FC DQN, trained from scratch with RL
setting.training_data: Online RL in 100 HM3D indoor scenes with randomized target and start positions; no extra or web data
setting.observation: RGBD frames with ground-truth object detections and perfect localization
setting.action_space: Macro actions (navigate to a map node), executed via A* and low-level elementary actions (turn/forward)
setting.privileged: Ground-truth object detection and perfect localization/SLAM; progress vector x_t giving the current target index

numbers_note: Results are given only as plots of steps per episode (Fig. results) versus a random macro-action baseline; no numeric table and no standard benchmark metrics such as SR/SPL.
results: The trained DQN agent consistently needs fewer elementary steps per episode than a random macro-action baseline for 1, 2 and 3 targets, with immediate and terminal rewards, and with both cylinder and real objects. The gap is largest under terminal reward. Results are qualitative (plots only), with no comparison to other published navigation methods.
limitations: Assumes perfect object detection, localization and idealized low-level navigation, and depends on handcrafted map-construction heuristics
Requires a hand-given progress vector; training has high wall-time and memory cost from many elementary steps and multiple patches per node
Evaluation only against a random baseline, with no quantitative table; the agent ignores map structure and its own location when choosing nodes
